vignette:
She is nineteen, a contemporary dancer who has spent most of her adolescence inside studios-counting beats under her breath, stretching before dawn, measuring herself against mirrors. Before the trauma, her life feels narrow in a way she likes: class, rehearsal, performances, part-time work at the front desk of the dance school, then home with sore muscles and the private satisfaction of getting stronger. She is single, living with her mother, and already imagines a future organized around companies, auditions, and touring. Her body is not just hers; it is her instrument, her discipline, and the way she understands herself.

The event happens at an indoor arts complex where she is attending a weekend workshop. It is crowded with students, teachers, parents, and performers moving between rehearsal rooms and a small theater. She remembers standing near a vending machine in her warm-up clothes, checking the time and rubbing resin off the bottom of one shoe. Then there is a blast-violent, metallic, and wrong. For a moment she does not understand it as an explosion, only as a force that throws sound and heat through the corridor and folds everyone into chaos. The lights go out. Fire alarms begin. People scream in different directions. Later she learns it is an intentional bombing, a man-made attack that tears through the lobby just as participants are changing rooms.

What she remembers most is not a clear sequence but fragments: the sting of dust in her eyes, someone falling against her shoulder, the smell of smoke and chemicals, a girl from another studio crying for her mother. She drops to the floor because others are dropping. She crawls, her palms sliding over broken glass and something wet she does not let herself identify. A teacher grabs the back of her sweatshirt and drags her toward an exit. Outside, in the cold air, she realizes she is barefoot. Sirens layer over each other. She keeps patting her own arms and legs, checking whether they are still there. Her left calf is cut, and her ears ring so loudly she cannot hear questions. She sees stretchers. She sees a man covered in dust standing perfectly still, as if he has forgotten how to move. For weeks afterward, that image returns to her with a force stronger than memory.

At first everyone tells her she is lucky. She is not killed. Her injuries are minor. She even returns to dance after a few weeks, though the cut on her calf pulls when she points her foot. She tries to believe she can step back into the life she had. Instead, the studio becomes unpredictable terrain. The slam of a heavy door makes her drop into a crouch before she can stop herself. During music changes, if the speakers crackle, her chest locks and she cannot catch her breath. She begins scanning every room for exits before she notices the choreography. In rehearsal, she loses counts she has known for years because part of her attention is always somewhere else, listening for danger.

Sleep changes next. She dreads it. When she does drift off, she wakes soaked in sweat, heart racing, the explosion happening again before she fully opens her eyes. Sometimes the dream is exact; sometimes it is only noise, smoke, and the certainty that she will die. She starts avoiding sleepovers, early train rides to auditions, crowded cafés after class. Her friends text and invite her out, but she leaves messages unanswered because she does not know how to explain why a busy room now feels unbearable. If someone comes up behind her unexpectedly, she spins around with her hands up, ashamed before she even understands what she is doing.

Dance, once the place where she feels most fluent, becomes tangled with fear and grief. She stares at herself in the mirror and feels estranged from her own body. The same body that used to feel precise and disciplined now feels jumpy, unreliable, too full of adrenaline. She grows angry when instructors tell her to "relax into the movement," as if she is choosing this stiffness. On certain combinations involving floor work, she freezes. Being low to the ground brings back the corridor, the broken glass, the pressure to keep crawling. She tells people her calf still hurts, which is sometimes true, but not the whole truth.

At home, her mother notices she keeps the television volume low and checks the locks repeatedly at night. She sits with her back to walls in restaurants. She studies strangers' hands, bags, shoes, as though clues might announce who is dangerous. News reports about attacks in other cities pull her in and repel her at the same time; she cannot stop reading them, then feels sick and shaky afterward. She is harder on herself than anyone else is. Nineteen feels, to her, too young to be this afraid and too old to need comforting.

Now, months later, she still speaks about life as divided into before and after. She goes to class, marks combinations, and sometimes even performs, but she moves through the day braced for another rupture. She wants the old certainty back-the simple trust that a building is just a building, that music will stay music, that her body belongs to dance and not to fear. Instead she lives with the sense that disaster can enter anywhere, at any time, and that some part of her is still in that corridor, barefoot in smoke, trying to find the exit.
